lessons.title: Understanding Event Propagation: Capturing vs Bubbling
lessons.description: Events travel through the DOM in two phases — understand how and why they propagate.

sections.heading: The three phases of event propagation
paragraphs: When you click an element, the event doesn't just fire on that element — it travels through the entire DOM tree. Understanding these phases prevents confusing bugs.
list: Capturing phase — the event travels down from the document root to the target element
Target phase — the event reaches the element you actually clicked
Bubbling phase — the event travels back up from the target to the document root
By default, listeners fire during the bubbling phase

codeExamples.heading: Bubbling in action
explanation: Clicking the inner element fires the click event on it first.
Then the event bubbles up to the parent, firing its listener too.
This is why both messages appear — the parent's listener also catches the event.

codeExamples.heading: Capturing phase listeners
explanation: Pass true as the third argument to listen during the capturing phase.
Capturing fires top-down: parent before child.
Bubbling fires bottom-up: child before parent.
Almost all code uses bubbling — capturing is rarely needed.

practice.task: Create a nested div structure (grandparent → parent → child). Add click listeners to all three. Click the innermost div and observe the order of log messages to see bubbling in action.
hints: Create three nested divs with different classes.
Add click listeners to each div.
Click the innermost div and note the console output order.

keyTakeaways: Events propagate in three phases: capturing (down), target, then bubbling (up).
By default, event listeners fire during the bubbling phase.
Bubbling causes parent elements to receive events from their children.
Pass true as the third argument to listen during the capturing phase.
lessons.challenge: Add both capturing and bubbling listeners on a parent and child. Log the phase in each handler to see the exact order events fire.

lessons.title: Stopping Event Propagation (stopPropagation)
lessons.description: Use stopPropagation() to prevent an event from reaching parent or child elements.

sections.heading: When bubbling causes problems
paragraphs: Sometimes you don't want an event to bubble up. For example, a modal overlay might have its own click handler, but clicking inside the modal content should not trigger the overlay's close handler.
list: event.stopPropagation() — stops the event from bubbling further
event.stopImmediatePropagation() — stops all remaining listeners on the same element
Use sparingly — it can break other code that relies on bubbling

codeExamples.heading: Using stopPropagation
explanation: stopPropagation() prevents the event from reaching parent elements.
The inner handler fires normally, but the outer handler never gets called.
The event is stopped at the point where stopPropagation() is called.

practice.task: Create a parent and child div with click listeners. Add stopPropagation to the child's listener so clicking the child doesn't trigger the parent's handler.
hints: Click the child — only the child's message should appear.
Click the parent — the parent's message should still work.

keyTakeaways: stopPropagation() prevents the event from reaching parent elements.
It stops the event at the current handler — earlier handlers in the same phase still fire.
Use it only when bubbling would cause unintended side effects.
stopImmediatePropagation() also prevents other listeners on the same element from firing.
lessons.challenge: Build a modal that closes when you click the backdrop, but stays open when you click inside the modal content. Use stopPropagation on the content.

lessons.title: Implementing the Event Delegation Pattern for Dynamic Lists
lessons.description: Attach one listener to a parent instead of many listeners to children — essential for dynamic content.

sections.heading: Why event delegation?
paragraphs: If you have a list with 100 items, adding a click listener to each one is inefficient. Worse, if you add new items dynamically, they won't have listeners. Event delegation solves both problems by using a single listener on the parent.
list: Attach one listener to a parent element
Use e.target to detect which child was clicked
New dynamically-added children are automatically handled
Uses event bubbling — the parent receives all child events

codeExamples.heading: Delegating click events on a list
explanation: One listener on the <ul> handles clicks on all <li> elements.
No need to add listeners to each item — even dynamically created ones work.
This is the standard pattern for handling events on lists and tables.

codeExamples.heading: Delegation with data attributes
explanation: Use data-* attributes to identify what each element should do.
The switch statement routes to the appropriate action.
One listener handles the entire menu — clean and maintainable.
New buttons with data-action are handled automatically.

practice.task: Create a to-do list with a "delete" button on each item. Use event delegation on the list container instead of adding individual listeners to each button.
hints: Attach the listener to the <ul>, not individual <li> elements.
Use e.target.closest("li").remove() to find and remove the parent item.

keyTakeaways: Event delegation uses one parent listener instead of many child listeners.
Use e.target to identify which child triggered the event.
Dynamically added elements are handled automatically — no re-attaching listeners.
Combine with data-* attributes for clean, scalable event handling.
lessons.challenge: Build a shopping cart with add/remove buttons for each item. Use event delegation so newly added items work without extra listeners.
